paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.8:1 Rule 10.8 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.8. 1. Consequences for Violating R. 10.7 In my opinion, a solicitor who fails to comply with RR. 616 and 617 should not be entitled to derive any benefit from his failure or omission. His position should be, in any event, no better than that of his colleague who complied with the rules. The solicitor who has complied with the rules is limited by the very terms of the contingency arrangement to a maximum recovery as set out in the contingency agreement. If the fees that might otherwise be charged on a quantum meruit basis exceed in quantum that allowable pursuant to the contingency, the solicitor who has complied with the rules is limited to recovery of the percentage set out in the contingency agreement. In my opinion, it necessarily follows that a lawyer who has not complied with RR. 616 and 617 should be in no better position … In my opinion, R. 618 is intended to operate so as to limit solicitors who have not complied with R. 616 to a fee recovery based upon quantum meruit if that fee calculation is less than the fee that would otherwise be payable pursuant to the contingency arrangement. Solicitors who have failed to comply with R. 616 and would otherwise have been entitled to a higher fee based on a contigency calculation have, by their conduct, lost that entitlement. Baergen v. Peterson Ross (1986), 48 Alta. L.R. (2d) 386 (Q.B.), at 390–91, per Berger J. In Leffler v. Collins (1997), 213 A.R. 395 (Q.B.), the lawyer billed the client on the basis of an oral, and therefore unfiled, contingency agreement. In ruling that the agreement was unenforceable, Veit J. said, at p. 396: It is only in the rarest of circumstances that the requirements of the rules relating to the requirement not only that contingency agreements be in writing, but also that they be filed, will be relaxed. It may be, for example, that a fully informed client may be able to effectively waive the benefit of those rules. In discussing when such a waiver would occur, Her Ladyship said, at pp. 397–98: It is, indeed, very likely that [the client] does understand the basis on which [the lawyer] agreed to act for her in these various proceedings. Nonetheless, the Rules establish not only the requirement that contingency agreements be in writing, and filed with the court, but also the treatment that shall be handed out when a contingency agreement does not comply with the Rules. It will be seen that rule 618 is not limited to those situations where the client, for example, understands the nature of the contingency arrangement. The rules applies in the broadest possible way: the reason for this is that the rule is designed to ensure compliance by lawyers with the requirements of rule 616. If the courts were to carve exceptions out of rule 618 for ordinary situations, the overall thrust of the requirement that contingency agreements be in writing and filed and thus subject on the one hand to advice from an independent lawyer and on the other to regulation by the courts would be greatly undermined. It is to foster that overall objective rather than to deal specifically with the situation here that the court subjects [the lawyer] to the general application of rule 618. Finally, as to quantum meruit, Veit J. said, at p. 397: The traditional response of the courts to oral contingency agreements has been to determine that they are unenforceable and that the lawyer should be able to recover only fees on a quantum meruit basis. As to what a quantum meruit basis is, the case law suggests that this is not equivalent to party and party costs as determined by the tariff established under the Rules. As Berger, J., as he then was, quoted with approval in Baergen … the extent and character of the services considered, and labour, time and trouble involved, the character and importance of the litigation in which the services were rendered, the amount of money or the value of the property involved, the professional skill and experience called for, the character and standing in his profession of the counsel and the results achieved. must all be taken into account in determining the amount of the lawyer's quantum meruit claim. 2. Court's Discretion to Waive Irregularities In Sonnenberg v. Schumacher & Associates, 2005 ABQB 352, 2005 CarswellAlta 840, 52 Alta. L.R. (4th) 151, 16 C.P.C. (6th) 88, Germain J. had before him a contingency agreement which did not strictly comply with Rule 616. As to the court's ability to waive such irregularities, his Lordship said, at pp. 156–157: The Sockett contingency agreement does comply for the most part with Rule 616, except that it does not contain the client's address. Rule 618 states that an agreement that does not comply with Rule 616 is to be disregarded. The courts do have a broad discretion to ignore irregularities, but Rule 618 has been interpreted very strictly. See, for example, Jackie & Handerek v. Dohmann 83 A.R. 308 (Alta. Q.B. 1987). I agree that Rule 618 purposefully prohibits enforcement when there is non-compliance, but I find that the Rule should not be interpreted so inflexibly that the most minuscule and immaterial omission would prevent the enforcement of the agreement. Therefore, even though I confirm that defects in a contingency agreement will be strictly construed against the lawyer, the court is not without its judicial discretion to alleviate against minor technical oversights that are without import. The failure of the agreement to set out the address of the client is one of those minor drafting irregularities that I would relieve against. However, here there are two more substantial irregularities. The next irregularity is the lack of an affidavit of execution on some copies of the agreement, including the copy that the client had and that was filed in the original taxation. Here, where the law firm was able to produce a properly signed copy, complete with an affidavit of execution, the fact that some copies did not have all affidavits attached is not an irregularity at all, or if so is insignificant. The second such irregularity is the lack of proof of the time of service on the client. The client acknowledged that she had a copy from somewhere, but did not know when or how she had received it. There is a suggestion that the client took the copy with her after signing the contingency agreement. The affidavit of service in this contingency agreement is not completed. Nevertheless, it would still be open for the lawyer to prove service in any way that would be recognized by the court. Here, due to the passage of time and the departure of personnel from the law firm, there is no absolute way to prove service as mandated by Rule 616(4). Applying a strict interpretation of this Rule based on the Alberta jurisprudence, this breach cannot be relieved against. Authority for this proposition is Jackie & Handerek, cited above. There, Miller A.C.J. dealt with the Rule as it read before it required proof of service on the client. Historically, any contingency agreement had to be filed at the courthouse. There, the contingency agreement was not so filed. When the Rule was amended in 2000, the filing requirement was abolished. Instead, there is now a requirement of proof of service and a cooling-off period for clients to change their mind without legal consequences. Miller A.C.J. found that the lack of filing at the courthouse precluded the enforcement of an otherwise valid agreement. So too I must find, that the lack of satisfactory proof of the timing and occurrence of service prevents the lawyer from relying on the contingency agreement to justify the account. In Niam v. Silverberg, 2015 ABQB 682, a client challenged the enforceability of a contingency fee agreement. Justice Brooker discussed the situations in which a contingency fee agreement (CFA) could survive non-compliance with the service requirement in the Rules. In the following excerpts, “CESPC” is the professional corporation of the lawyer. His Lordship said: 114 Both parties acknowledge that a signed copy of the CFA was never formally served on Niam. Rather, as discussed above, CESPC emailed the CFA (as executed by Silverberg on behalf of CESPC) to Glock and Niam on October 31, 2013, along with a full copy of Part 10 of the Rules. On November 4, 2013, Niam executed the agreement on her own behalf in the presence of a notary public, and provided a copy of the fully executed document to CESPC. 115 While Niam acknowledges having possession of a fully executed copy of the CFA as of November 3, 2013, she argues that CESPC failed to serve her with an executed version, and that this non-compliance is more than merely technical. Niam argues that Rule 10.7(4) expressly requires the lawyer to serve an executed version of a contingency fee agreement upon his or her client, and that the converse occurred in this instance. … 122 Interestingly, in the subsequent decision in Leffler, while the Court found that an agreement which had not been reduced to writing could not be relied upon, Veit J went on to state, at para 3: • The oral contingency agreement is not enforceable by Mr. Collins against Ms. Leffler. It is only in the rarest circumstances that the requirements of the rules relating to the requirement not only that contingency agreements be in writing, but also that they be filed, will be relaxed. It may be, for example, that a fully informed client may be able to effectively waive the benefit of those rules. This case is not exceptional. [emphasis added] 123 The above demonstrates the possible departure from the approach taken in Dohmann where the Court held that a failure to file would defeat the agreement. It further demonstrates a willingness to relax not only the more technical requirements of the rules (such as the filing requirement) but also the more substantive requirements, in certain circumstances. I am in full agreement with Justice Veit that the requirements contained in the rules may only be relaxed in exceptional cases. However, I find that the case before me is indeed exceptional, given Niam's sophistication coupled with the unique circumstances in which the CFA was drafted, revised, and ultimately presented to Niam. … 128 While I agree that the rules require service of a fully executed document, on the unique facts before me, it would be unreasonable to set aside the CFA simply because CESPC failed to return to Niam a copy of the exact document that Niam had just executed and provided to CESPC. In the circumstances, the final version of the CFA was provided to Niam and her counsel after an extensive period of negotiation and revision. A complete copy of Part 10 of the Rules was also provided. Niam then signed the agreement in the presence of a notary. This differs from the typical circumstances in which a contingency fee is provided to a client; i.e. a standard form agreement drafted solely by the lawyer and provided to the client after an initial consultation. Service, and the corresponding ability of the client to terminate the agreement upon further reflection, is much more important in conventional cases. 129 Thus, while I find formal service as mandated under the rules was not effected, the CFA was conveyed to Niam (and Glock) in a context in which it was clear that, by executing the document, certain rights and obligations were being engaged. While service was not technically effected as required by rule 10.7(4), I find this to be a rare instance where the failure to strictly comply with the rules does not result in the CFA being found unenforceable under rule 10.8. 130 A departure from the strict approach usually taken by the courts was recently seen in Botan (Botan Law Office) v St Amand, 2011 ABQB 774, 529 AR 313 (Michalyshyn J). In that case Mr. Botan sent his client (St. Amand) the firm's form of contingency fee agreement following a telephone discussion about St. Amand's possible claim. St. Amand signed the agreement and returned it to Botan. There was no service upon the client. In finding the contingency fee agreement valid, notwithstanding Botan's failure to strictly comply with the rules, this Court held as follows, at paras 42–44: • St. Amand argues the Agreement is invalid owing to a number of technical defects including that it was not dated or arguably signed, was not formally served on him, and was not appropriately witnessed in the sense that no one swore an affidavit attesting to his witness's signature. • Numerous cases were referred to regarding the need for strict though not perfect compliance with the form of contingency fee agreements and with former Rule 616: Morrison v. Rod Pantony Professional Corporation 2008 ABCA 145; Rusk v. Medicine Hat (City of) 2001 ABQB 1020; Sonnenberg v. Schumacher & Associates 2005 ABQB 352. • In all of the circumstances I would not invalidate the Agreement. The formalities around execution of a contingency fee agreement aim to avoid uncertainty and disputes as to what was agreed. Formal service of such an agreement creates a “cooling off” period enabling the client to walk away from the agreement without liability even for disbursements. Here the Agreement would have been no clearer to St. Amand with or without an affidavit of execution of the witness to St. Amand's signature or indeed with or without Botan's signature. And St. Amand was no worse off for the loss of the “cooling off” period that follows service. He could terminate the Agreement at any time before Botan submitted an application for compensation, without liability for fees and—given Botan's waiver of out-of-pocket expenses—without liability for disbursements. 131 Niam urges against placing any reliance upon Botan, arguing that it does not follow established jurisprudence. I find Botan to be of assistance in that it deals with a situation similar to that at bar, namely, the sole defect legitimately complained of is lack of service of a fully executed agreement. Moreover, Botan was confirmed by our Court of Appeal: 2013 ABCA 227. While the appeal dealt with an unrelated issue, the Court was silent as to Michalyshyn J's treatment of the enforceability of the contingency fee agreement. While Botan does appear to contemplate a departure from the rules even absent the “exceptional” circumstances called for in Loffler, it nevertheless demonstrates this Court's willingness to uphold agreements which might otherwise be set aside on “technical” defects. 132 On the unique facts of this case, I find that Niam is not able to rely on rule 10.8 to set aside the CFA, notwithstanding the fact that she was never formally served by CESPC with a fully executed copy of the agreement. 133 My conclusion is supported by the fact that Niam is not the type of client typically seen entering into contingency fee agreements. The overall aim of these types of agreements is to make court proceedings available to people who could not otherwise afford to have their legal rights determined: Coronation Insurance Co v Florence, [1994] SCJ No 116 (Cory J). As more recently commented upon by this Court in M(S) v D(M), at para 38: • That said, one must also consider that the people who rely on contingency fee arrangements are often vulnerable due to poverty, impact of injuries, educational status, or other social disadvantages. The Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010, Law Society Code of Conduct, and jurisprudence related to contingency fee agreements and other legal fee arrangements offer some protection for this potentially vulnerable segment of the population. 134 The nature of contingency fee agreements and the typical power imbalance between lawyer and client have led to what was described by Germain J in Sonnenberg, at para 30, as: • … the delicate balancing of public policy around contingency agreements which has led to their acceptance, but only under strict Rules to ensure fairness to both sides. If the strict Rules are followed, then the contingency is considered with much weight, on taxation. If the strict Rules are breached, then the contingency is not considered. 135 Niam's personal circumstances lessen the need for protection as historically recognized by the courts. The evidence demonstrates that Niam was in a position to fund her litigation without having to enter into a contingency fee arrangement. Indeed, she had already retained CESPC on a retainer for earlier services. In addition, there is no indication that Niam was otherwise vulnerable. In addition to possessing financial means, she is a worldly individual, she is politically connected, and she is highly educated. 136 Finally, Niam's situation is unusual in that she had independent legal counsel advocating on her behalf during the drafting and execution of the CFA. The courts have recognized an element of conflict of interest inherent in contingency fee agreements: see Oliver v Oliver (Public Trustee of) (1996), 18 BCLR (3d) 337 (BCCA) para 30. This conflict is lessened—at least during the agreement negotiation stage—by having independent counsel involved in drafting the agreement. The evidence in this case demonstrates that Glock had a high level of input during drafting. 137 The CFA is therefore enforceable notwithstanding CESPC's failure to formally to serve a fully executed copy of the document on Niam.

Right to Taxation of a Bill The applicant is correct in stating that the right of a person who has received a bill for professional services from an Alberta barrister or solicitor to tax that bill is a right of such importance that it can only be struck down or even whittled down in exceptional cases: rule 614, Alberta Rules of Court. U.A., Local 488 v. MacDonald (1987), 85 A.R. 283 (Q.B.), at 285, per Veit J. 2. Right to Taxation Exists for Client's Benefit The inherent jurisdiction of the court to tax accounts is for the benefit of the client, not the lawyer. The second argument I will deal with is the Applicants' suggestion that the Court's inherent jurisdiction to review solicitors' accounts, because of its general and inherent power over barristers and solicitors as officers of the Court, extends to an inherent right for a solicitor to have his or her account taxed. The cases cited in support of this proposition are Re E., [1922] 2 W.W.R. 1324 (Alta. C.A.), Smith, Hutchison & Gow v. Van't Reit (1985), 64 B.C.L.R. 41 (C.A.), Re T. (1921), 16 Alta. L.R. 449 (C.A.), and M. v. T. (1962), 40 W.W.R. 623 (Alta. T.D.) … In all four cases the Courts confirmed the inherent jurisdiction of the Court to review solicitors' accounts at the request of the client. As I read these cases they do not confirm an inherent right for a solicitor to have his or her account taxed. P., Barristers & Solicitors v. Legal Aid Society (Alberta) (1994), 26 Alta. L.R. (3d) 167 (Q.B.), at 173–74, per Fruman J. At p. 174, her Ladyship went on to note that lawyers tax accounts for different reasons from clients. She said: Solicitors … elect to have their accounts to their clients taxed as a step in an expedited collection procedure. That is not the only avenue for collection open to them. I do not think that the same public policy reasons apply or that the Court's inherent jurisdiction to tax extends to a counsel's inherent right to use an expedited collection procedure. Similarily, the same public policy reasons do not extend to a lawyer who has by contract agreed to accept some other collection procedure instead of the taxation procedure. 3. A Lawyer May Contract out of R. 10.9 A lawyer, in contradistinction to a client, may contract out of the provisions of R. 10.9. Therefore, a lawyer who has agreed to conduct a file through the financial auspices of Legal Aid may not resort to the rule for the purpose of collecting fees. By placing themselves on the Legal Aid roster and ultimately signing certificates in respect of their representation of the two accused individuals, the Applicants contractually committed themselves to be bound by the Tariff and the Legal Aid Rules. Those Legal Aid Rules set out a detailed procedure for the submission of accounts, approval of accounts by the Taxation Officer of the Legal Aid Society and appeals to the Exceptional Accounts Review Committee, whose decision is final. The Applicants not only accepted those terms by signing the certificate, they acted in furtherance of those terms by submitting accounts in accordance with the Legal Aid Rules and exhausting the available appeals. They now turn to the Courts for a taxation in furtherance of their collection of the outstanding accounts from the Legal Aid Society. Where, as here, a solicitor, with full knowledge and understanding, has accepted a tariff of fees and a procedure for their assessment and payment, it would be inequitable and inappropriate to read R. 614 as permitting the solicitor to, in effect, breach his or her contractual commitments and apply to the Courts for the taxation of fees, in furtherance of collection. … I conclude that a solicitor may not have an account rendered to the Legal Aid Society pursuant to a certificate taxed under the Rules of Court. Lawyers are bound by the Tariff and collection procedures set out in the Legal Aid Rules. P., Barristers & Solicitors v. Legal Aid Society (Alberta) (1994), 26 Alta. L.R. (3d) 167 (Q.B.), at 174–75, 177, per Fruman J. 4. Reason for Rule The reasons for the taxation of legal fees by a client are fundamentally different than the reasons for taxation by a lawyer. The client, after all, is liable to pay the fees. He or she may be concerned that they are excessive or want independent confirmation that they are reasonable. The client may be legally unsophisticated. He or she might not be able to assess the value of the services received and might contractually agree not to tax an account without fully understanding the implications. Barristers and solicitors are officers of the Court and the Court retains an inherent jurisdiction to assess the reasonableness of their fees even though a client has waived that right by contract. Under R. 614 the charges of barristers and solicitors are therefore “subject to” taxation. P., Barristers & Solicitors v. Legal Aid Society (Alberta) (1994), 26 Alta. L.R. (3d) 167 (Q.B.), at 174, per Fruman J. 5. Taxing Officer May Not Determine Questions of Liability “The taxing officer's jurisdiction is limited to determining quantum, not liability. What the terms of a contract are is a question of fact. That question cannot be decided where the contract is a verbal and there is a dispute about its terms. Like any other contract a dispute about the terms must be resolved by a judicial officer of the court.”Peterson, Ross v. Kirkwood (1984), 52 A.R. 284 (Master), at 289, per Master Funduk, quoting Gilbert v. Douglas Rentals Ltd. (26th July 1983), Edmonton Q.B. 8303-15325 (unreported). And in another decision, Master Funduk stated: Where there is an issue about the measuring stick to be used to measure compensation there is no point in the taxing officer proceeding to still tax the account. In Peterson, Ross v. Kirkwood (1984), 52 A.R. 284, it is stated at p. 290: If an issue had been raised about liability the taxing officer clearly could not have dealt with it, other than possibly procedurally. He could have referred the issue to a Judge in Chambers: Rule 634. He could have not dealt with it at all procedurally, leaving the parties to take whatever steps they might consider appropriate. If an issue had been raised about the measuring stick to be used to measure the compensation the taxing officer could not have decided that issue, and accordingly could not have decided quantum. In that case he has the same choice as in the preceding paragraph: refer the matter to a Judge or decline to tax the bill on the ground of lack jurisdiction, thus leaving the parties to take whatever steps they might consider appropriate. In my view, generally it would be the most appropriate step for the taxing officer to refer the issue as to what measuring stick to use to a Judge in chambers, under Rule 634. Lennie, De Bow & Martin v. Richter (1984), 55 A.R. 26 ((Master)), at 28, per Master Funduk. 6. “Reasonableness of a lawyer's charges” In Steinke v. Hajduk Gibbs LLP, 2014 ABQB 34, 2014 CarswellAlta 77, 581 A.R. 91, 96 Alta. L.R. (5th) 155, Justice Wakeling discussed the factors to be considered when determining the “reasonableness of a lawyer's charges”. His Lordship said: 43 Rule 10.9 of the Alberta Rules of Court stipulates that the “reasonableness of a lawyer's charges are subject to review by a review officer in accordance with these rules, despite any agreement to the contrary”. 44 It follows that a lawyer's charges must be reasonable. 45 This part of my judgment explores the meaning of this norm. 46 In Alberta Treasury Branches v. 1401057 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748 I recorded the ten general principles governing court-ordered costs payable inter partes. Many of these principles also serve as general principles governing fees paid by a client to a lawyer.6 My reasons for judgment in Alberta Treasury Branches and this case may usefully be read together. 47 The first principle governing the review of an account submitted by a lawyer to a client directs the Court of Queen's Bench to review, if asked by the client or the lawyer, the amounts a lawyer has charged a client for legal services the client retained the lawyer to perform. … … 49 The second principle is based on the fact that a lawyer who is a member of The Law Society of Alberta cannot charge a client more than a “fair and reasonable” amount. Code of Conduct 2.06(1) (2013). This is an ethical obligation of which almost all lawyers are keenly aware.8 See W. Stevenson & J. Côté, Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook 2013–2014 at 10.5. 50 A review officer must be mindful of this ethical obligation when assessing a lawyer's charges. There is a presumption that a lawyer will act in accordance with the Code of Conduct when she submits an account to the client.9 See McLennan Ross v. Keen Industries Ltd., 83 A.R. 322, 323 (C.A. 1987) (“the account of the solicitor must … be considered by the taxing officer as the solicitor's conscientious estimate of the value of the work performed by him”). This is the second principle. A review officer who, exercising authority under r. 10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court, reduces a fee because it exceeds a fair and reasonable amount is asserting that a lawyer is in breach of this obligation. 51 The third principle is that a court must hold the lawyer and the client to promises made in a retainer agreement10 regarding amounts a lawyer may charge and a client must pay for legal services in the absence of a compelling reason not to.11 Rule 10.5 of the Alberta Rules of Court is the Alberta provision with embodies this basic principle. It states that “[a] lawyer may make an agreement with a client about the amount and the manner of payment of the whole or any part of past or future lawyer's charges for services performed by the lawyer”. The significance of a retainer agreement, which is a defined term in the Alberta Rules of Court, is emphasized in r. 10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court. This subrule provides the criteria which determines the amount a client must pay the lawyer for legal services performed by the lawyer unless a retainer agreement sets out the criteria which serve this purpose. Canadian Legal Practice: A Guide for the 21st Century 40.48 (A. Dodek gen. ed. looseleaf release 24 September 2013) (“Where lawyers and clients have not agreed on the amount to be charged on fees for required legal work, the lawyer's entitlement is determined on a quantum meruit basis”). Rule 10.2(1) introduces a reasonableness measure shaped by four specific but hard-to-apply factors (“(a) the nature, importance and urgency of the matter, (b) the client's circumstances, … (d) the manner in which the services are performed, (e) the skill, work and responsibility involved”) and one omnibus and equally abstract factor (“any other factor that is appropriate to consider in the circumstances”), the combined effect of which is to turn the assessment process into a forensic lottery. It is safe to say that adjudicators asked to apply these factors are seldom likely to come up with similar conclusions as to what is a reasonable amount. In other words, the value of this process is not predictability and certainty. … The value of the process is finality—the dispute is resolved. 52 The fourth principle is that a court taxing a lawyer's charges to a client must act in a principled manner. “The absence of … logical framework introduces arbitrariness and uncertainty. Its presence promotes rationality and consistency”. Alberta Treasury Branches v. 1401057 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748, para 28. … This judgment provides an analytical framework for the review of contested lawyer charges. A review officer properly exercises her jurisdiction if she is guided by principle.12 53 If there is no retainer agreement or there is no provision in a retainer agreement relating to amounts a lawyer may charge, or the retainer agreement stipulates that a lawyer's charges will be fair and reasonable, r. 10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court kicks in. It declares, as previously noted, that “a lawyer is entitled to be paid a reasonable amount for the services the lawyer performs for a client”. To discharge its obligation under the fourth principle, the Court must apply the criteria listed in r. 10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court and provide an explanation as to how they influenced the adjudicator's decision13. … 54 If there is a provision in a retainer agreement which clearly14 states that r. 10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court does not apply and substitutes a different formula, the court must apply the norm contained in the retainer agreement to determine the entitlement of the lawyer and the obligation of the client. McDonald Crawford v. Morrow, 348 A.R. 118, 132 (C.A. 2004) (“A court must interpret a contract as whole [in order to ascertain the compensation formula]”). 55 The retainer agreement will identify the legal services the client retained the lawyer to perform and the methodology of assessing the lawyer's fee.15 56 Seldom is there a dispute about the nature of the legal services for which the lawyer is entitled to be paid.16 This is so whether or not there is a retainer agreement. The client and the lawyer usually had a common understanding as to the purpose of the retainer. It may have been representing the client at a trial or an appeal or drafting a contract. 57 Controversy is most likely to attach to legal services which the client claims were not necessary to perform or which the client asserts took too much time to perform. 58 The fifth and the sixth principles are designed to resolve controversies of this nature. 59 The fifth principle is that unless there is a contrary provision in the retainer agreement, a client must pay for a legal service which increases the likelihood the purpose of the retainer agreement will be achieved.17 If the client retained a lawyer to oppose an appeal, the review officer must ask whether the contested legal service increased the likelihood the appeal court would dismiss the appeal. 60 In Alberta Treasury Branches v. 1401057 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748, para 39 I commented on this concept in the context of inter partes costs: [39] The requirement that a legal service increases the likelihood the purpose stipulated … is achieved is a low standard. It may be less demanding than some of the tests adopted by other courts. But I am not sure Other courts have preferred slightly different wording. The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, in Fleck v. Whitehead, [1924] S.J. No. 84, …, approved fees if they related to steps “properly” or “necessarily” undertaken. In Royal Bank of Canada v. Toews, [2007] S.J. No. 173, …[the Saskatchewan Court of Queen's Bench] asked if a step was “appropriate, necessary and reasonable in the circumstances” or was “properly …[taken] to recover the mortgage money”. … Much earlier, the Admiralty Court in The Kestrel, … (1867) determined that recoverable costs are those necessary to protect the mortgagee's interest. Most of the time the two different tests—increase the likelihood of success or necessary for the proper presentation—will produce the same outcome. But I can envisage fact patterns where they might not. Suppose that [law firm] C had three counsel appear on an appeal. Some review officers may agree that the presence of three counsel—each may have different areas of expertise which may be needed to answer questions from the court—may increase the likelihood [client] B would prevail on the appeal but would not be necessary for the proper presentation of the case. They may be of the view that the likelihood the court will pose questions to lead counsel which she cannot answer is too low to justify the extra cost associated with the presence of two other lawyers. …Others may be convinced that the presence of three highly skilled counsel may be necessary for the proper presentation of a complex appeal. Kirkwood v. Webster, 9 Ch.D. 241 … (H.C. 1878) (the court set aside the Taxing Master's decision disallowing costs for three counsel because “a reasonable and prudent man … would not have ventured to come into Court without three counsel”); Ed Miller Sales & Rental Ltd. v. Caterpillar Tractor Co., 216 A.R. 304, 306 (C.A. 1998) (“If ever there was a suit which did not call for penny-pinching half measures by the defendant, this was it”) …. 61 These observations apply equally to the assessment of the appropriate amount a client must pay its lawyer. A client who agrees to pay a lawyer on a time spent basis cannot reasonably be held responsible for time a lawyer devotes to activities which do not increase the likelihood the purpose of the retainer will be achieved. … 62 In passing, I observe that work performed may increase the likelihood the purpose of the retainer will be achieved even if the result of the legal service indicates that a potential argument is unsound. … 63 The sixth principle, generally speaking, is that a client is not responsible for the cost associated with unnecessary steps.18 This means that if a contested step is adjudged to increase the likelihood that the purpose of the retainer will be attained, it may still be a step for which the client cannot be held responsible if it is adjudged to be unnecessary. An unnecessary step is one for which the value derived from the step is much less than the cost of completing it. Alberta Treasury Branches v. 14010507 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748, para 41. … But a review officer should not substitute her view of what is an appropriate expenditure of client resources for that of the lawyer unless the law firm's expenditure decision is clearly indefensible.19 This is a very important qualification to bear in mind when considering the sixth principle. The client retained the lawyer to make these strategic decisions and should be responsible for the costs consequences of these decisions. Alberta Treasury Branches v. 14010507 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748, para 41; Credit Fancier Trust Co. v. Hornigold, 45 Alta. L.R. (2d) 341, 348 (Q.B. 1984) &Andrukow Group Solutions (Ryley) Inc. v. Evergreen Farms Ltd., Alta. Q.B. Action No. 1103 07615, at 71 (Q.B. Assessment Officer October 20, 2011) (the assessment officer lamented the fact that he did not have current market information about the cost of providing comparable legal services). The sixth principle is not a general invitation to a review officer to second guess counsel's judgment calls. See The Queen v. G.D.B., [2000] 1 S.C.R. 520, 532 (“The wisdom of hindsight has no place in this assessment”). She may only conclude that a step is unnecessary if counsel's decision is clearly indefensible. 64 The seventh principle is that a client who instructs a lawyer to take a step which increases the likelihood the objective of the retainer will be achieved but will not likely present a benefit which justifies the cost or does not increase the likelihood of success is responsible for the fees associated with this extraordinary service. … 65 A client who instructs a lawyer to leave no stone unturned in the pursuit of the objective of the retainer agreement cannot complain when his lawyer complies with the direction and devotes time to the undertaking just because either the benefit associated with the extraordinary measures did not meet the client's expectations or cost more than the client foresaw. … 66 The eighth principle directs a court “to ensure that those who are obliged to pay for legal services are treated reasonably, taking into account all the circumstances”. Alberta Treasury Branches v. 1401057 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748, para 43. … 67 The key question in applying the eighth principle is this: Are the law firm's charges exorbitant so that it can be said the law firm has taken advantage of its clients? … In answering this query the Court is not conducting a r. 10.2(1) analysis. The eighth principle serves a completely different purpose than r. 10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court. 68 As there is an increased risk that an unsophisticated consumer of legal services may be taken advantage of, a court, in reviewing a lawyer's relationship with such a client, will exercise its protective function with more vigour than will be the case if the client is a regular consumer of legal services and familiar with the issues which arise in the delivery of legal services. This is because a sophisticated client has the necessary skills to protect its own interests when transacting professional business with lawyers. Alberta Treasury Branches v. 1401057 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748, para 43. … 69 The eighth principle plays no role if the parties have not agreed upon a compensation model and a lawyer's charges are determined by applying r 10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court. There is no need to ask if a law firm has taken advantage of a client by charging an exorbitant fee once a review officer has settled on a reasonable amount. An amount which is adjudged to be reasonable cannot also be exorbitant. 70 The likelihood that charges based on a timekeeper model and are compliant with the fifth and sixth principles will run afoul of the eighth principle is extremely low. Fees which are incurred as a result of services that increase the likelihood the purpose of the retainer will be achieved and the cost of incurring them is less than the value derived from the service are not a sign a lawyer has taken advantage of her client. 71 The eighth principle is more likely to be engaged if a lawyer and a client have agreed to a fixed or contingency fee arrangement. … 72 The ninth principle requires the client who contests his or her lawyer's charges at the outset of the hearing to particularize his or her complaint. A client who has not agreed to a formula which determines the amount a lawyer may charge and is thus obliged to pay a reasonable amount for legal services, in accordance with r. 10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court, must state that the amount charged is unreasonable and why. A client who has agreed to a formula which determines the amount a lawyer may charge, as is the case in these appeals, must explain the basis of her objection. Does she take the position that the lawyer seeks compensation for services which did not increase the likelihood the subject of the retainer would be achieved? Does she claim that a service was unnecessary even though it increased the likelihood the object of the retainer would be met? Or does she claim that the charges violate the eighth principle—that the lawyer's charges are exorbitant so that it can be said the lawyer has taken advantage of the client. Bhatnager v. Canada, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 317, 319 &Holmes Greenslade v. Starcom International Optics Corp., 14 C.P.C. (4th) 388, 392 (B.C. Sup. Ct. 1997). This obligation rests on the client because of the second principle—there is a presumption that a lawyer will not submit an account to a client which is inconsistent with an obligation under the Code of Conduct not to charge more than an amount which is fair and reasonable. Proceeding without a particularization of the client's complaint is unfair to the lawyer. The lawyer cannot address the client's concerns if he does not know what they are. Fair play demands nothing less. 73 The tenth principle is that the lawyer bears the burden of persuading the review officer that the amount charged is appropriate. … If appropriateness of the amount charged is measured by r. 10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court, the lawyer must convince the review officer that the amount charged is reasonable considering the factors listed in r. 10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court. If, as in this fact pattern, the appropriateness of the amount charged is a function of the time spent by designated service providers and their hourly rates, the law firm must be prepared to explain why the services performed increased the likelihood [of success]; why the services were necessary; and that the amount charged is not exorbitant.

10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court, reduces a fee because it exceeds a fair and reasonable amount is asserting that a lawyer is in breach of this obligation.

51 The third principle is that a court must hold the lawyer and the client to promises made in a retainer agreement10 regarding amounts a lawyer may charge and a client must pay for legal services in the absence of a compelling reason not to.11 Rule 10.5 of the Alberta Rules of Court is the Alberta provision with embodies this basic principle.

It states that “[a] lawyer may make an agreement with a client about the amount and the manner of payment of the whole or any part of past or future lawyer's charges for services performed by the lawyer”.
The significance of a retainer agreement, which is a defined term in the Alberta Rules of Court, is emphasized in r.
10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court.

This subrule provides the criteria which determines the amount a client must pay the lawyer for legal services performed by the lawyer unless a retainer agreement sets out the criteria which serve this purpose.
Canadian Legal Practice: A Guide for the 21st Century 40.48 (A.

Dodek gen. ed. looseleaf release 24 September 2013) (“Where lawyers and clients have not agreed on the amount to be charged on fees for required legal work, the lawyer's entitlement is determined on a quantum meruit basis”).
Rule 10.2(1) introduces a reasonableness measure shaped by four specific but hard-to-apply factors (“(a) the nature, importance and urgency of the matter
(b) the client's circumstances, …
(d) the manner in which the services are performed

(e) the skill, work and responsibility involved”) and one omnibus and equally abstract factor (“any other factor that is appropriate to consider in the circumstances”), the combined effect of which is to turn the assessment process into a forensic lottery.
It is safe to say that adjudicators asked to apply these factors are seldom likely to come up with similar conclusions as to what is a reasonable amount.
In other words, the value of this process is not predictability and certainty. … The value of the process is finality—the dispute is resolved.
52 The fourth principle is that a court taxing a lawyer's charges to a client must act in a principled manner. “The absence of … logical framework introduces arbitrariness and uncertainty.
Its presence promotes rationality and consistency”.
Alberta Treasury Branches v.
1401057 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748, para 28. … This judgment provides an analytical framework for the review of contested lawyer charges.

A review officer properly exercises her jurisdiction if she is guided by principle.12 53 If there is no retainer agreement or there is no provision in a retainer agreement relating to amounts a lawyer may charge, or the retainer agreement stipulates that a lawyer's charges will be fair and reasonable, r.
10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court kicks in.
It declares, as previously noted, that “a lawyer is entitled to be paid a reasonable amount for the services the lawyer performs for a client”.
To discharge its obligation under the fourth principle, the Court must apply the criteria listed in r.

10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court and provide an explanation as to how they influenced the adjudicator's decision13. … 54 If there is a provision in a retainer agreement which clearly14 states that r.

10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court does not apply and substitutes a different formula, the court must apply the norm contained in the retainer agreement to determine the entitlement of the lawyer and the obligation of the client.
McDonald Crawford v.
Morrow, 348 A.R.
2004) (“A court must interpret a contract as whole [in order to ascertain the compensation formula]”).

55 The retainer agreement will identify the legal services the client retained the lawyer to perform and the methodology of assessing the lawyer's fee.15 56 Seldom is there a dispute about the nature of the legal services for which the lawyer is entitled to be paid.16 This is so whether or not there is a retainer agreement.
The client and the lawyer usually had a common understanding as to the purpose of the retainer.
It may have been representing the client at a trial or an appeal or drafting a contract.
57 Controversy is most likely to attach to legal services which the client claims were not necessary to perform or which the client asserts took too much time to perform.
58 The fifth and the sixth principles are designed to resolve controversies of this nature.

59 The fifth principle is that unless there is a contrary provision in the retainer agreement, a client must pay for a legal service which increases the likelihood the purpose of the retainer agreement will be achieved.17 If the client retained a lawyer to oppose an appeal, the review officer must ask whether the contested legal service increased the likelihood the appeal court would dismiss the appeal.
60 In Alberta Treasury Branches v.

1401057 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748, para 39 I commented on this concept in the context of inter partes costs: [39] The requirement that a legal service increases the likelihood the purpose stipulated … is achieved is a low standard.
It may be less demanding than some of the tests adopted by other courts.
But I am not sure Other courts have preferred slightly different wording.
The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, in Fleck v.
Whitehead, [1924] S.J.
No.
84, …, approved fees if they related to steps “properly” or “necessarily” undertaken.
In Royal Bank of Canada v.
Toews, [2007] S.J.
No.

173, …[the Saskatchewan Court of Queen's Bench] asked if a step was “appropriate, necessary and reasonable in the circumstances” or was “properly …[taken] to recover the mortgage money”. … Much earlier, the Admiralty Court in The Kestrel, …
(1867) determined that recoverable costs are those necessary to protect the mortgagee's interest.
Most of the time the two different tests—increase the likelihood of success or necessary for the proper presentation—will produce the same outcome.
But I can envisage fact patterns where they might not.
Suppose that [law firm] C had three counsel appear on an appeal.

Some review officers may agree that the presence of three counsel—each may have different areas of expertise which may be needed to answer questions from the court—may increase the likelihood [client] B would prevail on the appeal but would not be necessary for the proper presentation of the case.

They may be of the view that the likelihood the court will pose questions to lead counsel which she cannot answer is too low to justify the extra cost associated with the presence of two other lawyers. …Others may be convinced that the presence of three highly skilled counsel may be necessary for the proper presentation of a complex appeal.
Kirkwood v.
Webster, 9 Ch.D.

1878) (the court set aside the Taxing Master's decision disallowing costs for three counsel because “a reasonable and prudent man … would not have ventured to come into Court without three counsel”); Ed Miller Sales & Rental Ltd. v.
Caterpillar Tractor Co., 216 A.R.
1998) (“If ever there was a suit which did not call for penny-pinching half measures by the defendant, this was it”) ….
61 These observations apply equally to the assessment of the appropriate amount a client must pay its lawyer.

A client who agrees to pay a lawyer on a time spent basis cannot reasonably be held responsible for time a lawyer devotes to activities which do not increase the likelihood the purpose of the retainer will be achieved. … 62 In passing, I observe that work performed may increase the likelihood the purpose of the retainer will be achieved even if the result of the legal service indicates that a potential argument is unsound. … 63 The sixth principle, generally speaking, is that a client is not responsible for the cost associated with unnecessary steps.18 This means that if a contested step is adjudged to increase the likelihood that the purpose of the retainer will be attained, it may still be a step for which the client cannot be held responsible if it is adjudged to be unnecessary.
An unnecessary step is one for which the value derived from the step is much less than the cost of completing it.
Alberta Treasury Branches v.

14010507 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748, para 41. … But a review officer should not substitute her view of what is an appropriate expenditure of client resources for that of the lawyer unless the law firm's expenditure decision is clearly indefensible.19 This is a very important qualification to bear in mind when considering the sixth principle.
The client retained the lawyer to make these strategic decisions and should be responsible for the costs consequences of these decisions.
Alberta Treasury Branches v.
14010507 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748, para 41; Credit Fancier Trust Co. v.
Hornigold, 45 Alta.
L.R.
1984) &Andrukow Group Solutions (Ryley) Inc. v.
Evergreen Farms Ltd., Alta.
Q.B.
Action No.

The sixth principle is not a general invitation to a review officer to second guess counsel's judgment calls.
See The Queen v.
520, 532 (“The wisdom of hindsight has no place in this assessment”).
She may only conclude that a step is unnecessary if counsel's decision is clearly indefensible.

10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court.

Canada, [1991] 3 S.C.R.

Sup.
Ct.

The lawyer cannot address the client's concerns if he does not know what they are.

Right to Taxation of a Bill The applicant is correct in stating that the right of a person who has received a bill for professional services from an Alberta barrister or solicitor to tax that bill is a right of such importance that it can only be struck down or even whittled down in exceptional cases: rule 614, Alberta Rules of Court. U.A., Local 488 v. MacDonald (1987), 85 A.R. 283 (Q.B.), at 285, per Veit J. 2. Right to Taxation Exists for Client's Benefit The inherent jurisdiction of the court to tax accounts is for the benefit of the client, not the lawyer. The second argument I will deal with is the Applicants' suggestion that the Court's inherent jurisdiction to review solicitors' accounts, because of its general and inherent power over barristers and solicitors as officers of the Court, extends to an inherent right for a solicitor to have his or her account taxed. L.R. 449 (C.A.), and M. v. T. (1962), 40 W.W.R. 623 (Alta. T.D.) … In all four cases the Courts confirmed the inherent jurisdiction of the Court to review solicitors' accounts at the request of the client. As I read these cases they do not confirm an inherent right for a solicitor to have his or her account taxed. P., Barristers & Solicitors v. Legal Aid Society (Alberta) (1994), 26 Alta. L.R. (3d) 167 (Q.B.), at 173–74, per Fruman J. At p. 174, her Ladyship went on to note that lawyers tax accounts for different reasons from clients. Similarily, the same public policy reasons do not extend to a lawyer who has by contract agreed to accept some other collection procedure instead of the taxation procedure. 3. The Applicants not only accepted those terms by signing the certificate, they acted in furtherance of those terms by submitting accounts in accordance with the Legal Aid Rules and exhausting the available appeals. They now turn to the Courts for a taxation in furtherance of their collection of the outstanding accounts from the Legal Aid Society. (3d) 167 (Q.B.), at 174–75, 177, per Fruman J. 4. Reason for Rule The reasons for the taxation of legal fees by a client are fundamentally different than the reasons for taxation by a lawyer. The client may be legally unsophisticated. He or she might not be able to assess the value of the services received and might contractually agree not to tax an account without fully understanding the implications. Barristers and solicitors are officers of the Court and the Court retains an inherent jurisdiction to assess the reasonableness of their fees even though a client has waived that right by contract. (3d) 167 (Q.B.), at 174, per Fruman J. 5. Taxing Officer May Not Determine Questions of Liability “The taxing officer's jurisdiction is limited to determining quantum, not liability. Right to Taxation of a Bill The applicant is correct in stating that the right of a person who has received a bill for professional services from an Alberta barrister or solicitor to tax that bill is a right of such importance that it can only be struck down or even whittled down in exceptional cases: rule 614, Alberta Rules of Court.
U.A., Local 488 v.
MacDonald (1987), 85 A.R.
283 (Q.B.), at 285, per Veit J.
Right to Taxation Exists for Client's Benefit The inherent jurisdiction of the court to tax accounts is for the benefit of the client, not the lawyer.

The second argument I will deal with is the Applicants' suggestion that the Court's inherent jurisdiction to review solicitors' accounts, because of its general and inherent power over barristers and solicitors as officers of the Court, extends to an inherent right for a solicitor to have his or her account taxed.
The cases cited in support of this proposition are Re E., [1922] 2 W.W.R.
1324 (Alta.
C.A.), Smith, Hutchison & Gow v.
Van't Reit (1985), 64 B.C.L.R.
L.R.
449 (C.A.), and M. v.
T.
623 (Alta.
T.D.) … In all four cases the Courts confirmed the inherent jurisdiction of the Court to review solicitors' accounts at the request of the client.
As I read these cases they do not confirm an inherent right for a solicitor to have his or her account taxed.
P., Barristers & Solicitors v.
Legal Aid Society (Alberta) (1994), 26 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 167 (Q.B.), at 173–74, per Fruman J.
At p.
174, her Ladyship went on to note that lawyers tax accounts for different reasons from clients.
She said: Solicitors … elect to have their accounts to their clients taxed as a step in an expedited collection procedure.
That is not the only avenue for collection open to them.
I do not think that the same public policy reasons apply or that the Court's inherent jurisdiction to tax extends to a counsel's inherent right to use an expedited collection procedure.
Similarily, the same public policy reasons do not extend to a lawyer who has by contract agreed to accept some other collection procedure instead of the taxation procedure.
A Lawyer May Contract out of R.
10.9 A lawyer, in contradistinction to a client, may contract out of the provisions of R.
Therefore, a lawyer who has agreed to conduct a file through the financial auspices of Legal Aid may not resort to the rule for the purpose of collecting fees.

By placing themselves on the Legal Aid roster and ultimately signing certificates in respect of their representation of the two accused individuals, the Applicants contractually committed themselves to be bound by the Tariff and the Legal Aid Rules.

Those Legal Aid Rules set out a detailed procedure for the submission of accounts, approval of accounts by the Taxation Officer of the Legal Aid Society and appeals to the Exceptional Accounts Review Committee, whose decision is final.

The Applicants not only accepted those terms by signing the certificate, they acted in furtherance of those terms by submitting accounts in accordance with the Legal Aid Rules and exhausting the available appeals.
They now turn to the Courts for a taxation in furtherance of their collection of the outstanding accounts from the Legal Aid Society.

Where, as here, a solicitor, with full knowledge and understanding, has accepted a tariff of fees and a procedure for their assessment and payment, it would be inequitable and inappropriate to read R.

614 as permitting the solicitor to, in effect, breach his or her contractual commitments and apply to the Courts for the taxation of fees, in furtherance of collection. … I conclude that a solicitor may not have an account rendered to the Legal Aid Society pursuant to a certificate taxed under the Rules of Court.
Lawyers are bound by the Tariff and collection procedures set out in the Legal Aid Rules.
P., Barristers & Solicitors v.
Legal Aid Society (Alberta) (1994), 26 Alta.
L.R.

The client, after all, is liable to pay the fees.
He or she may be concerned that they are excessive or want independent confirmation that they are reasonable.
The client may be legally unsophisticated.
He or she might not be able to assess the value of the services received and might contractually agree not to tax an account without fully understanding the implications.
Barristers and solicitors are officers of the Court and the Court retains an inherent jurisdiction to assess the reasonableness of their fees even though a client has waived that right by contract.
Under R.
614 the charges of barristers and solicitors are therefore “subject to” taxation.

Legal Aid Society (Alberta) (1994), 26 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 167 (Q.B.), at 174, per Fruman J.
Taxing Officer May Not Determine Questions of Liability “The taxing officer's jurisdiction is limited to determining quantum, not liability.
What the terms of a contract are is a question of fact.
That question cannot be decided where the contract is a verbal and there is a dispute about its terms.
Like any other contract a dispute about the terms must be resolved by a judicial officer of the court.”Peterson, Ross v.
Kirkwood (1984), 52 A.R.
284 (Master), at 289, per Master Funduk, quoting Gilbert v.
Douglas Rentals Ltd.
(26th July 1983), Edmonton Q.B.
8303-15325 (unreported).

In Peterson, Ross v.

284, it is stated at p.
290: If an issue had been raised about liability the taxing officer clearly could not have dealt with it, other than possibly procedurally.
He could have referred the issue to a Judge in Chambers: Rule 634.
He could have not dealt with it at all procedurally, leaving the parties to take whatever steps they might consider appropriate.
If an issue had been raised about the measuring stick to be used to measure the compensation the taxing officer could not have decided that issue, and accordingly could not have decided quantum.

In that case he has the same choice as in the preceding paragraph: refer the matter to a Judge or decline to tax the bill on the ground of lack jurisdiction, thus leaving the parties to take whatever steps they might consider appropriate.
In my view, generally it would be the most appropriate step for the taxing officer to refer the issue as to what measuring stick to use to a Judge in chambers, under Rule 634.

Richter (1984), 55 A.R.
26 ((Master)), at 28, per Master Funduk.
6. “Reasonableness of a lawyer's charges” In Steinke v.

91, 96 Alta.

(5th) 155, Justice Wakeling discussed the factors to be considered when determining the “reasonableness of a lawyer's charges”.

His Lordship said: 43 Rule 10.9 of the Alberta Rules of Court stipulates that the “reasonableness of a lawyer's charges are subject to review by a review officer in accordance with these rules, despite any agreement to the contrary”.
44 It follows that a lawyer's charges must be reasonable.
45 This part of my judgment explores the meaning of this norm.
46 In Alberta Treasury Branches v.
1401057 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748 I recorded the ten general principles governing court-ordered costs payable inter partes.

Many of these principles also serve as general principles governing fees paid by a client to a lawyer.6 My reasons for judgment in Alberta Treasury Branches and this case may usefully be read together.

47 The first principle governing the review of an account submitted by a lawyer to a client directs the Court of Queen's Bench to review, if asked by the client or the lawyer, the amounts a lawyer has charged a client for legal services the client retained the lawyer to perform. … … 49 The second principle is based on the fact that a lawyer who is a member of The Law Society of Alberta cannot charge a client more than a “fair and reasonable” amount.
Code of Conduct 2.06(1) (2013).
This is an ethical obligation of which almost all lawyers are keenly aware.8 See W.
Stevenson & J.
Côté, Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook 2013–2014 at 10.5.

Keen Industries Ltd., 83 A.R.

This is the second principle.
A review officer who, exercising authority under r.
10.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court, reduces a fee because it exceeds a fair and reasonable amount is asserting that a lawyer is in breach of this obligation.

51 The third principle is that a court must hold the lawyer and the client to promises made in a retainer agreement10 regarding amounts a lawyer may charge and a client must pay for legal services in the absence of a compelling reason not to.11 Rule 10.5 of the Alberta Rules of Court is the Alberta provision with embodies this basic principle.

It states that “[a] lawyer may make an agreement with a client about the amount and the manner of payment of the whole or any part of past or future lawyer's charges for services performed by the lawyer”.
The significance of a retainer agreement, which is a defined term in the Alberta Rules of Court, is emphasized in r.

This subrule provides the criteria which determines the amount a client must pay the lawyer for legal services performed by the lawyer unless a retainer agreement sets out the criteria which serve this purpose.

Alberta Treasury Branches v.

The client and the lawyer usually had a common understanding as to the purpose of the retainer.
It may have been representing the client at a trial or an appeal or drafting a contract.

No.

No.

Some review officers may agree that the presence of three counsel—each may have different areas of expertise which may be needed to answer questions from the court—may increase the likelihood [client] B would prevail on the appeal but would not be necessary for the proper presentation of the case.

Kirkwood v.
Webster, 9 Ch.D.

1878) (the court set aside the Taxing Master's decision disallowing costs for three counsel because “a reasonable and prudent man … would not have ventured to come into Court without three counsel”); Ed Miller Sales & Rental Ltd. v.

L.R.
1984) &Andrukow Group Solutions (Ryley) Inc. v.

Q.B.
Action No.

520, 532 (“The wisdom of hindsight has no place in this assessment”).

Kirkwood (1984), 52 A.R. 284, it is stated at p. 290: If an issue had been raised about liability the taxing officer clearly could not have dealt with it, other than possibly procedurally. Morrow, 348 A.R. 118, 132 (C.A. 2004) (“A court must interpret a contract as whole [in order to ascertain the compensation formula]”). 55 The retainer agreement will identify the legal services the client retained the lawyer to perform and the methodology of assessing the lawyer's fee.15 56 Seldom is there a dispute about the nature of the legal services for which the lawyer is entitled to be paid.16 This is so whether or not there is a retainer agreement. The client and the lawyer usually had a common understanding as to the purpose of the retainer. It may have been representing the client at a trial or an appeal or drafting a contract. 57 Controversy is most likely to attach to legal services which the client claims were not necessary to perform or which the client asserts took too much time to perform. 58 The fifth and the sixth principles are designed to resolve controversies of this nature. 59 The fifth principle is that unless there is a contrary provision in the retainer agreement, a client must pay for a legal service which increases the likelihood the purpose of the retainer agreement will be achieved.17 If the client retained a lawyer to oppose an appeal, the review officer must ask whether the contested legal service increased the likelihood the appeal court would dismiss the appeal. 60 In Alberta Treasury Branches v. 1401057 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 748, para 39 I commented on this concept in the context of inter partes costs: [39] The requirement that a legal service increases the likelihood the purpose stipulated … is achieved is a low standard. Canada, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 317, 319 &Holmes Greenslade v. Starcom International Optics Corp., 14 C.P.C. (4th) 388, 392 (B.C. Sup. Ct. 1997). This obligation rests on the client because of the second principle—there is a presumption that a lawyer will not submit an account to a client which is inconsistent with an obligation under the Code of Conduct not to charge more than an amount which is fair and reasonable. Proceeding without a particularization of the client's complaint is unfair to the lawyer. The lawyer cannot address the client's concerns if he does not know what they are. Right to Taxation of a Bill The applicant is correct in stating that the right of a person who has received a bill for professional services from an Alberta barrister or solicitor to tax that bill is a right of such importance that it can only be struck down or even whittled down in exceptional cases: rule 614, Alberta Rules of Court. U.A., Local 488 v. MacDonald (1987), 85 A.R. 283 (Q.B.), at 285, per Veit J. 2. Right to Taxation Exists for Client's Benefit The inherent jurisdiction of the court to tax accounts is for the benefit of the client, not the lawyer. The second argument I will deal with is the Applicants' suggestion that the Court's inherent jurisdiction to review solicitors' accounts, because of its general and inherent power over barristers and solicitors as officers of the Court, extends to an inherent right for a solicitor to have his or her account taxed. The cases cited in support of this proposition are Re E., [1922] 2 W.W.R. 1324 (Alta. C.A.), Smith, Hutchison & Gow v. Van't Reit (1985), 64 B.C.L.R. 41 (C.A.), Re T. (1921), 16 Alta. L.R. 449 (C.A.), and M. v. T. (1962), 40 W.W.R. 623 (Alta. T.D.) … In all four cases the Courts confirmed the inherent jurisdiction of the Court to review solicitors' accounts at the request of the client. As I read these cases they do not confirm an inherent right for a solicitor to have his or her account taxed. P., Barristers & Solicitors v. Legal Aid Society (Alberta) (1994), 26 Alta. L.R. (3d) 167 (Q.B.), at 173–74, per Fruman J. At p. 174, her Ladyship went on to note that lawyers tax accounts for different reasons from clients. She said: Solicitors … elect to have their accounts to their clients taxed as a step in an expedited collection procedure. That is not the only avenue for collection open to them. I do not think that the same public policy reasons apply or that the Court's inherent jurisdiction to tax extends to a counsel's inherent right to use an expedited collection procedure. Similarily, the same public policy reasons do not extend to a lawyer who has by contract agreed to accept some other collection procedure instead of the taxation procedure. 3. A Lawyer May Contract out of R. 10.9 A lawyer, in contradistinction to a client, may contract out of the provisions of R. 10.9. Therefore, a lawyer who has agreed to conduct a file through the financial auspices of Legal Aid may not resort to the rule for the purpose of collecting fees. By placing themselves on the Legal Aid roster and ultimately signing certificates in respect of their representation of the two accused individuals, the Applicants contractually committed themselves to be bound by the Tariff and the Legal Aid Rules. Those Legal Aid Rules set out a detailed procedure for the submission of accounts, approval of accounts by the Taxation Officer of the Legal Aid Society and appeals to the Exceptional Accounts Review Committee, whose decision is final. The Applicants not only accepted those terms by signing the certificate, they acted in furtherance of those terms by submitting accounts in accordance with the Legal Aid Rules and exhausting the available appeals. They now turn to the Courts for a taxation in furtherance of their collection of the outstanding accounts from the Legal Aid Society. Where, as here, a solicitor, with full knowledge and understanding, has accepted a tariff of fees and a procedure for their assessment and payment, it would be inequitable and inappropriate to read R. 614 as permitting the solicitor to, in effect, breach his or her contractual commitments and apply to the Courts for the taxation of fees, in furtherance of collection. … I conclude that a solicitor may not have an account rendered to the Legal Aid Society pursuant to a certificate taxed under the Rules of Court. Lawyers are bound by the Tariff and collection procedures set out in the Legal Aid Rules. P., Barristers & Solicitors v. Legal Aid Society (Alberta) (1994), 26 Alta. L.R. (3d) 167 (Q.B.), at 174–75, 177, per Fruman J. 4. Reason for Rule The reasons for the taxation of legal fees by a client are fundamentally different than the reasons for taxation by a lawyer. The client, after all, is liable to pay the fees. He or she may be concerned that they are excessive or want independent confirmation that they are reasonable. The client may be legally unsophisticated. He or she might not be able to assess the value of the services received and might contractually agree not to tax an account without fully understanding the implications. Barristers and solicitors are officers of the Court and the Court retains an inherent jurisdiction to assess the reasonableness of their fees even though a client has waived that right by contract. Under R. 614 the charges of barristers and solicitors are therefore “subject to” taxation. P., Barristers & Solicitors v. Legal Aid Society (Alberta) (1994), 26 Alta. L.R. (3d) 167 (Q.B.), at 174, per Fruman J. 5. Taxing Officer May Not Determine Questions of Liability “The taxing officer's jurisdiction is limited to determining quantum, not liability. What the terms of a contract are is a question of fact. That question cannot be decided where the contract is a verbal and there is a dispute about its terms.
